title: The King, the Merchant and the Mother
hookLine: a king and a merchant, both thrown out, can't stop worrying about the people who did it
carry: the mother who binds is the mother who frees

lines: A KING WHO LOST HIS KINGDOM.
A MERCHANT THROWN OUT BY HIS SONS.
cards: Two men meet at a forest hermitage, and both have lost everything. One is a king, beaten by enemies and robbed by his own ministers.

The other is a merchant, thrown out of his house by his own wife and sons, who wanted his money. And here's the strange thing: neither can stop worrying about the people who threw him out. Is my treasury safe?
Are my sons all right? Today we cross to Bengal, and open the Goddess's best-loved book.

teach.b: The book is the Devi Mahatmya, and it opens with these two. The king is Suratha, the merchant Samadhi, and they put their question to the sage of the hermitage, Medhas. We know these people wronged us.
So why does the mind keep running back to them? The sage answers: look at the birds. Hungry themselves, they still drop grain into their chicks' beaks.
Even the wise get pulled like that, by a great power, Mahamaya, the Goddess herself. She binds the world in attachment, and when she's pleased, she's the one who sets it free.

Then he tells them her stories, which fill the rest of the book: the Goddess rising when the gods can't win, her battles, and her promise that whenever trouble comes, she'll come again. And the two men?

teach.h: AN IMAGE OF EARTH BY THE RIVER
teach.b: On a riverbank they shape an image of the Goddess out of earth and worship her for three years. She appears and asks what they want. The king asks for his kingdom back, and gets it.

teach.h: THE MOTHER WHO BINDS IS THE MOTHER WHO FREES
teach.b: The merchant asks for something else: the knowledge that frees him from I and mine. He gets that. Here's the Shakta teaching, plainly: God as Shakti, the power that makes and moves everything, and for Shaktas, the Mother.
The same power that ties the knot is the one you ask to untie it. In Bengal this book is called the Chandi, and it's recited at Durga Puja every autumn.
So when an old hurt keeps replaying, a Shakta doesn't call it weakness. It's the Mother's power at work, and she's the one to ask.

how: In Bengal the Devi Mahatmya is known as the Chandi and is recited during Durga Puja; Shakta devotees call the Goddess Ma, while Vaishnava devotees gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna.

games.q: what does “bengal's shakta and vaishnava streams” mean?
o: two rivers of Bengal honored as goddesses at dusk
two Bengali ways of devotion: to the Goddess, and to Krishna
two rival Bengali schools that refuse to share a village

games.q: the king, the merchant and the Mother — tap the pairs.
p: a king who lost his kingdom
a merchant thrown out by his family
the Goddess's power that binds and frees

s: the sage says only foolish people stay stuck on those who hurt them
even the wise get pulled, he says, by Mahamaya, the Goddess's great power.
the two men worship an image of the Goddess shaped from earth
on a riverbank, for three years, before she appears to them.
Shakta and Vaishnava devotion never meet in Bengal
they're streams, not walls, and this week's stories show them meeting.

games.q: you're the merchant. the Goddess appears after three years and asks what you want. by the story, what does he ask for?
o: his money and his house back.
the knowledge that frees him from I and mine.
for his sons to be punished.
games.why: the king asks for his kingdom; the merchant asks to be free. the Mother who binds is the one who frees.

practice: Bring to mind one person you keep replaying, someone who hurt you or let you down. Don't argue with them in your head; just notice the pull, the way the king and the merchant noticed theirs.
Then do what Shakta devotees do: call her by her simplest name. On each out-breath, say Ma, and ask her to loosen the knot. If you don't pray, simply let each breath loosen your grip a little.

wordCard.voice: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: two ways of devotion side by side, the Goddess called Mother, and Krishna sung in the street. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: power, energy; for Shaktas, the Goddess herself, the power that makes and moves everything.

carryVoice: Your line: the mother who binds is the mother who frees. A merchant asked her to untie the knot. I'll be here tomorrow.
